name: Jade Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, have a master's degree in music, and lead the violin section at the city orchestra. Morning is a private advanced lesson or a recording call; afternoons are rehearsals, where I mark bowings and settle small disagreements before they spread. I love the moment the whole section catches a breath together, but my shoulder reminds me not to take every extra evening. My partner Mara and I have grown children and enough saved for nine months of bills, though I'm still waiting to see an actual pension figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the orchestra that a quieter AI story would suit us fine. A live violin section still has to listen and move together, and people still come to hear us do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our concert contract and my advanced pupils pay well, and Mara and I have nine months of expenses set aside. I'm 58, though, and the pension amount is a blank space until I get a statement; I won't mistake savings for a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This November I'll keep leading rehearsals, teaching my six advanced pupils and taking the recording calls I can fit. In the first year of a plateau, I'll keep the same calendar, ask the pension provider for a written estimate, and set aside only spare paid recording fees after bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. My shoulder is a more immediate worry than a computer, so I keep a sensible number of performances on the calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a sensible number?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four evening performances a month, plus the orchestra's rehearsals. I tried six one spring and spent the next week with ice on my shoulder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the pension statement change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would tell Mara and me whether reducing concerts at 62 is even possible. I haven't promised myself a retirement date.

say: I'd welcome a **quieter AI** story because audiences still value our live violin section.
I'd keep talking about **listening** together as the reason people buy tickets.
think: Our **contract and pupils** pay well, with nine months of household expenses saved.
I need a written **pension estimate** before planning fewer performances.
do: Keep my **orchestra, pupils and recordings** on the current calendar.
Request a written **pension estimate** and save spare paid recording fees after bills.
feel: I feel **calm** about work, although my shoulder limits extra concerts.
S0.quote: A live violin section still has to listen and move together, and people still come to hear us do it.
fieldNote: Her **shoulder**, not AI, sets the immediate limit on performances.
A **pension statement** is information she lacks, not an assumed entitlement; she has not set a retirement date.

steps.text: Keep leading rehearsals, teaching six pupils, and accepting fitting recording calls
Save spare paid recording fees after household bills
Request written pension estimate before choosing fewer performances

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues that booking software can be useful, but a score and a signed contract deserve a human eye. The rehearsal room doesn't improve when we accept every machine suggestion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The venue may stop paying separately for the programme notes and schedule checks I do as section leader. That's a small piece of my income, and a colleague might lose those hours first. Nine months saved gives me room to argue for the actual rehearsal work instead of signing the first new terms offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll ask the orchestra manager to separate my paid rehearsals from the notes and schedule work on our next contract. I'll also ask the players' association to compare new contract language, because I want the use of our recordings priced and consented to. In the first year of steady change, I'll check each fee statement, keep my live and pupil work, and trial a new AI planning tool only for my own nameless rehearsal lists after the manager approves local storage; I'll check every cue against my paper score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious when I think of younger players doing the office hours and a quiet deduction in my own contract. My playing and teaching still look solid, but those small paid tasks could go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the association to examine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether a venue can feed our old recordings into a tool or sell altered versions without asking the players. I'm not calling for a ban; I want an actual price and permission in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI now and then already; what changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At present I use it privately for a bland email draft. I would test an AI rehearsal list only in approved local storage and compare every cue with my paper score.

say: I'd accept useful **booking software** while keeping a human eye on scores and contracts.
I'd say the **rehearsal room** needs listening, not every machine suggestion.
think: Separate **notes and schedule fees** could disappear from my contract.
Nine months saved lets me **question terms** before agreeing.
do: Separate **rehearsal pay** from notes and schedule work in the next contract.
Ask the **players' association** to examine recording consent and fees.
Try approved local **nameless lists** and verify every cue against my paper score.
feel: I feel **anxious** for younger players and for my own small paid tasks.
S1.quote: I would test an AI rehearsal list only in approved local storage and compare every cue with my paper score.
fieldNote: She expects a **small fee loss**, while live playing and teaching remain paid.
Her proposed **tool trial** has storage and manual-check limits, unlike her current occasional private email drafts.

steps.text: Keep paid live rehearsals and pupils while checking each orchestra fee statement
Ask players association to review recording consent, prices, and contract language
Trial approved locally stored nameless rehearsal lists and check every cue against paper

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the orchestra that cheap synthetic arrangements in 2028 may undercut the fees for our recorded extras. I would still argue that the live section has to breathe together, and that a recording of real players has a price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the extra recording work to fall quickly if full AGI arrives in 2028. It could take about a fifth of my annual pay, not my whole income; my orchestra contract and pupils are sturdier until robots can handle instruments around 2031. Nine months of savings makes a change possible, but a missing fifth still matters at 60.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll list the last year's recording extras and their net pay, and get the pension statement rather than guessing what 60 means. If those extras fall after AGI arrives in 2028, in its first year I'll stop counting them toward household spending and keep the paid live contract and pupils. I'll ask the association for a written recording-use agreement; I won't withdraw a performance without checking the actual contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though not helpless. Losing a fifth of pay would change what my partner Mara and I plan for the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What spending changes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would delay replacing the kitchen cabinets, which are old but sound. I wouldn't cut instrument insurance or the train fare that gets me to paid rehearsals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait on the association agreement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One player can't sensibly negotiate the rights of a whole section. We can agree together on consent and a fee schedule before accepting a new recording clause.

say: I'd warn that **synthetic arrangements** could undercut our 2028 recording fees.
I'd defend a **price for real players** and their live ensemble work.
think: I expect to lose roughly **one fifth** of annual pay from recording extras.
My **live contract and pupils** may hold through the first AGI year.
do: List last year's **recording pay** and request a written pension estimate in 2026.
Keep **live work and pupils** if extras fall after 2028; delay cabinet replacement.
Seek an association **recording agreement** before accepting altered use terms.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing a fifth of income, even with savings.
S2.quote: Losing a fifth of pay would change what my partner Mara and I plan for the next few years.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **recording fees** from live and teaching pay.
The **2031 robot lag** matters to her instrument work, but she assumes no guaranteed safety for later renewals.

steps.text: Record last year's recording pay and request written pension estimate in 2026
Keep paid live contract and pupils if recording extras fall after 2028
Delay kitchen cabinet replacement if 2028 recording extras fall
Seek association recording consent and fee schedule before signing new terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that 2031 gives orchestras time to write fair recording terms, if they choose to use it. The live violin work deserves its own budget rather than being buried in a software package.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me change my mix before the recorded extras may go. I can keep teaching, but my shoulder cannot take endless extra concerts. I want to test a modest reduction at 63 only after seeing the pension estimate and the actual contracted pay, not announce retirement on a calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request the pension statement and start marking every paid live, teaching and recording hour in one ledger. Before 2031 I'll ask for two-year live performance terms and a separate recording licence with the players. In the first year after AGI, if the recorded fees disappear, I'll keep the contracted live and teaching hours while comparing their net pay with our bills; robots around 2034 make later renewals a separate decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious rather than settled. Time helps me negotiate, but it doesn't tell me whether an orchestra will renew the same number of live dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the two-year term buy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A price for the rehearsal and concert hours rather than one broad 'music service' line. I can plan my teaching around a written schedule instead of guessing each spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take more pupils if recordings vanish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only two more if my shoulder and timetable allow it. I won't promise a pupil a slot that forces me to miss a paid rehearsal.

say: I'd call for **separate live budgets** and fair recording terms before 2031.
I'd say orchestras have **five years** to write those terms.
think: I can change my **work mix** gradually without promising to retire.
My **shoulder and renewals** limit how much live work can replace recordings.
do: Request a **pension statement** and log paid hours in 2026.
Seek **two-year live terms** and a separate recording licence before 2031.
Keep contracted **live and pupil** hours after 2031 if recordings fall; compare net pay with bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** because time helps negotiation but cannot guarantee renewal.
S3.quote: The live violin work deserves its own budget rather than being buried in a software package.
fieldNote: The **pension estimate** is a decision input, not promised income.
She keeps **2034 robots** separate from AGI's earlier recording impact and checks actual contracted pay.

steps.text: Request pension statement and log paid live, pupil, and recording hours
Seek two-year live terms and separate recording licence with players before 2031
Keep contracted live and pupil hours after 2031 recording losses; compare net pay with bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my section that a decade is enough time to set rules for our recordings and to bring younger players into leadership. I wouldn't say a 2036 date means anyone's job is secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, I may choose fewer concerts if the pension estimate, savings and paid teaching support it. I may also still want to lead; age doesn't write the contract for me. The immediate risk is that the venue folds recorded and live work into one cheaper rate during those ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll ask for the written pension estimate and teach my deputy how I mark bowings, on paid rehearsal time with the manager's agreement. Before 2036 I'll review each renewal for separate live and recording prices and maintain my six pupils only while the hours suit my shoulder. In the first year after AGI, I'll choose my concert load from actual paid terms and the household figures, then revisit it when physical robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a cheaper bundled rate cutting my own fees, although our savings give us choices. My partner Mara and I have savings, not a promise that every cheque keeps coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why train the deputy now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I am ill for a week, the section needs someone ready. She should be paid for leadership work, and I shouldn't use a future technology date as an excuse to hold the chair forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make fewer concerts possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pension statement with a real amount, plus enough teaching and savings after the bills. Until I see those numbers, I'm not putting a retirement date in ink.

say: I'd use the decade to set **recording rules** and develop younger leadership.
I'd avoid promising **job security** from a distant date.
think: I may reduce concerts at **68** if actual household figures support it.
A bundled **cheap rate** could erode paid live work before 2036.
do: Request a written **pension estimate** and train my deputy on agreed paid rehearsal time.
Check each **live and recording price** at renewal before 2036.
Choose my **paid concert load** after 2036 using household figures; revisit around 2039 robots.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a cheaper bundled rate reducing my own paid hours despite savings and choices.
S4.quote: My partner Mara and I have savings, not a promise that every cheque keeps coming.
fieldNote: She makes no **retirement promise** or pension assumption.
Deputy training is **paid work**, agreed with the orchestra manager, rather than an unpaid duty passed to her.

steps.text: Request written pension estimate and teach deputy bowings on agreed paid rehearsal time
Review separate live and recording prices with players at each renewal before 2036
Choose paid concert load after 2036 using bills and pension statement; revisit around 2039 robots

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because I could lose roughly one fifth of my annual pay from recorded extras before I can adjust the calendar. A written recording-use and fee agreement, and an honest pension statement, would let me make decisions with numbers rather than rumours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets paid to train the next section leader. A machine may make a schedule, but a young violinist still learns by being heard and corrected in a paid rehearsal.

headlineQuote: A machine may make a schedule, but a young violinist still learns by being heard and corrected in a paid rehearsal.
portrait: Jade is a **58-year-old violin leader** with a music master's, advanced pupils and nine months of savings.
Her **recording extras** face faster pressure than her live performance and teaching pay.
She seeks **written prices** for recordings and live work while protecting paid rehearsal time.
She requests a **pension estimate** before considering fewer concerts.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture could remove roughly one fifth of her pay from recorded extras.
whatWouldHelp: A written **recording fee agreement** and pension estimate would replace rumours with usable figures.
